sections.title: Dict Comprehension — Swapping Keys & Values — Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Conceptual Question:

**Q: What happens when you swap keys and values in a dict and values are not unique? How do you handle this properly?**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Level):**
> "When values are not unique and you swap, you get a **data loss** bug — only the last item for each duplicate value survives. This is a silent bug that doesn't raise an error, which makes it dangerous:
>
> ```python
> # DANGEROUS — silent data loss!
> roles = {'alice': 'admin', 'bob': 'user', 'carol': 'admin', 'dave': 'user'}
> role_to_user = {v: k for k, v in roles.items()}
> print(role_to_user)  # {'admin': 'carol', 'user': 'dave'}
> # alice and bob are silently gone!
> ```
>
> Solutions depending on use case:
>
> **1. One-to-many: group into lists** (most common):
> ```python
> from collections import defaultdict
> role_to_users = defaultdict(list)
> for user, role in roles.items():
>     role_to_users[role].append(user)
> # {'admin': ['alice', 'carol'], 'user': ['bob', 'dave']}
> ```
>
> **2. Check uniqueness before swapping**:
> ```python
> def safe_invert(d: dict) -> dict:
>     if len(set(d.values())) != len(d):
>         raise ValueError(f'Cannot invert dict with duplicate values')
>     return {v: k for k, v in d.items()}
> ```
>
> **3. Keep first occurrence (not last)**:
> ```python
> seen = set()
> role_to_user_first = {
>     v: k for k, v in roles.items()
>     if v not in seen and not seen.add(v)
> }
> ```
>
> In production, I always assert uniqueness before inverting or use the `defaultdict(list)` pattern. The silent overwrite is a common source of hard-to-debug data inconsistencies."

### Scenario Questions:

**Scenario 1: "You have an enum-like dict for error codes. Build a reverse mapping for logging human-readable messages."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Error code reverse lookup — I build this in every production service:
>
> ```python
> from enum import IntEnum
>
> class ErrorCode(IntEnum):
>     SUCCESS          = 0
>     INVALID_INPUT    = 1001
>     UNAUTHORIZED     = 1002
>     NOT_FOUND        = 1003
>     RATE_LIMITED     = 1004
>     DB_ERROR         = 2001
>     EXTERNAL_API     = 2002
>     TIMEOUT          = 2003
>
> # Human-readable messages
> ERROR_MESSAGES = {
>     ErrorCode.SUCCESS:        'Success',
>     ErrorCode.INVALID_INPUT:  'Invalid input provided',
>     ErrorCode.UNAUTHORIZED:   'Authentication required',
>     ErrorCode.NOT_FOUND:      'Resource not found',
>     ErrorCode.RATE_LIMITED:   'Too many requests — please retry later',
>     ErrorCode.DB_ERROR:       'Database error occurred',
>     ErrorCode.EXTERNAL_API:   'External service unavailable',
>     ErrorCode.TIMEOUT:        'Request timed out',
> }
>
> # Reverse: message → code (for parsing logs)
> MESSAGE_TO_CODE = {v: k for k, v in ERROR_MESSAGES.items()}
>
> # HTTP status code mapping
> CODE_TO_HTTP = {
>     ErrorCode.SUCCESS:        200,
>     ErrorCode.INVALID_INPUT:  400,
>     ErrorCode.UNAUTHORIZED:   401,
>     ErrorCode.NOT_FOUND:      404,
>     ErrorCode.RATE_LIMITED:   429,
>     ErrorCode.DB_ERROR:       500,
>     ErrorCode.EXTERNAL_API:   502,
>     ErrorCode.TIMEOUT:        504,
> }
>
> def format_error(code: ErrorCode) -> dict:
>     return {
>         'code':    int(code),
>         'message': ERROR_MESSAGES.get(code, 'Unknown error'),
>         'http_status': CODE_TO_HTTP.get(code, 500)
>     }
>
> print(format_error(ErrorCode.NOT_FOUND))
> # {'code': 1003, 'message': 'Resource not found', 'http_status': 404}
>
> # Parse log line to get error code
> log_message = 'Rate limited — Too many requests — please retry later'
> code = MESSAGE_TO_CODE.get('Too many requests — please retry later')
> print(f'Parsed code: {code}')  # ErrorCode.RATE_LIMITED (1004)
> ```"

**Scenario 2: "You're parsing a legacy system's field mappings. Old field names need to map to new names AND vice versa."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Legacy migration field mapping — classic in system modernization:
>
> ```python
> # Legacy field name → new field name
> FIELD_MIGRATION_MAP = {
>     'cust_nm':    'customer_name',
>     'cust_addr1': 'address_line_1',
>     'cust_addr2': 'address_line_2',
>     'cust_city':  'city',
>     'cust_state': 'state',
>     'cust_zip':   'postal_code',
>     'cust_ph':    'phone',
>     'cust_em':    'email',
>     'ord_dt':     'order_date',
>     'ord_amt':    'order_amount',
>     'ord_stat':   'order_status',
> }
>
> # Build reverse immediately:
> REVERSE_MIGRATION = {v: k for k, v in FIELD_MIGRATION_MAP.items()}
>
> def migrate_record(record: dict, direction: str = 'old_to_new') -> dict:
>     '''Transform a record between legacy and modern field names'''
>     mapping = FIELD_MIGRATION_MAP if direction == 'old_to_new' else REVERSE_MIGRATION
>     return {
>         mapping.get(field, field): value   # Use mapped name or keep original
>         for field, value in record.items()
>     }
>
> # Legacy record from old system
> legacy_record = {
>     'cust_nm': 'Alice Johnson',
>     'cust_city': 'New York',
>     'ord_dt': '2024-01-15',
>     'ord_amt': 299.99,
>     'ord_stat': 'shipped',
> }
>
> # Migrate to new format
> modern_record = migrate_record(legacy_record, 'old_to_new')
> print(modern_record)
> # {'customer_name': 'Alice Johnson', 'city': 'New York',
> #  'order_date': '2024-01-15', 'order_amount': 299.99, 'order_status': 'shipped'}
>
> # Send back to legacy system
> legacy_back = migrate_record(modern_record, 'new_to_old')
> print(legacy_back)
> # {'cust_nm': 'Alice Johnson', 'cust_city': 'New York', ...}
>
> # Verify round-trip integrity
> assert legacy_back == legacy_record, 'Round-trip migration failed!'
> print('✅ Round-trip migration verified')
> ```"

**Scenario 3: "In a URL shortener service, build both short→long and long→short lookup dicts."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "URL shortener bidirectional mapping:
>
> ```python
> import hashlib
> import time
>
> class URLShortener:
>     def __init__(self):
>         self._short_to_long = {}
>         self._long_to_short = {}
>
>     def shorten(self, long_url: str) -> str:
>         # Return existing short URL if already mapped
>         if long_url in self._long_to_short:
>             return self._long_to_short[long_url]
>
>         # Generate short code
>         hash_input = f'{long_url}{time.time()}'.encode()
>         short_code = hashlib.md5(hash_input).hexdigest()[:7]
>         short_url = f'https://short.ly/{short_code}'
>
>         # Store in both directions
>         self._short_to_long[short_url]  = long_url
>         self._long_to_short[long_url]   = short_url
>         return short_url
>
>     def expand(self, short_url: str) -> str | None:
>         return self._short_to_long.get(short_url)
>
>     def bulk_import(self, url_pairs: dict) -> None:
>         '''Import existing pairs using dict comprehension'''
>         self._short_to_long.update(url_pairs)
>         # Build reverse via dict comprehension swap
>         self._long_to_short.update({v: k for k, v in url_pairs.items()})
>
>     def stats(self) -> dict:
>         return {
>             'total_urls': len(self._short_to_long),
>             'mappings': {
>                 'short_to_long': len(self._short_to_long),
>                 'long_to_short': len(self._long_to_short),
>             }
>         }
>
> shortener = URLShortener()
>
> # Add URLs
> s1 = shortener.shorten('https://www.example.com/very/long/path?param=value')
> s2 = shortener.shorten('https://github.com/user/repo/blob/main/README.md')
>
> print(f'Short URL: {s1}')
> print(f'Expanded:  {shortener.expand(s1)}')
> print(f'Stats:     {shortener.stats()}')
>
> # Bulk import from database
> existing_pairs = {
>     'https://short.ly/abc1234': 'https://google.com',
>     'https://short.ly/def5678': 'https://github.com',
> }
> shortener.bulk_import(existing_pairs)
> print(f'After import: {shortener.stats()}')
> ```"

sections.title: Dict Comprehension — From Two Lists (zip) — Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Conceptual Question:

**Q: When would you use `dict(zip(keys, values))` versus `{k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)}`?**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Level):**
> "Both produce identical results for simple cases, but I choose based on what I need to do:
>
> **`dict(zip(keys, values))`** — cleanest, most readable when you JUST want a simple key-value mapping with no transformation:
> ```python
> headers = ['id', 'name', 'score']
> row = [1, 'Alice', 95]
> record = dict(zip(headers, row))  # Clean and obvious
> ```
>
> **`{k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values)}`** — when you need transformation, filtering, or conditional logic:
> ```python
> # Transform values during creation
> {k: v.strip().lower() for k, v in zip(keys, values) if v is not None}
>
> # Filter out None values
> {k: v for k, v in zip(keys, values) if v is not None}
>
> # Type conversion
> {k: int(v) for k, v in zip(keys, values)}
> ```
>
> In practice, I see `dict(zip())` most often in data parsing (CSV rows → record dicts) and `{k: v for k, v in zip()}` in transformation pipelines. I default to `dict(zip())` for readability and only add the comprehension syntax when I need extra logic.
>
> One gotcha I always mention in reviews: if the two lists might have different lengths, check first:
> ```python
> assert len(keys) == len(values), f'Length mismatch: {len(keys)} keys, {len(values)} values'
> result = dict(zip(keys, values))
> ```
> Silent truncation from mismatched lengths is a subtle bug."

### Scenario Questions:

**Scenario 1: "You parse CSV files where the first row is headers. Build a list of dicts from the data rows."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "CSV parsing with zip is a daily task:
>
> ```python
> import csv
> from io import StringIO
>
> csv_content = '''id,product_name,price,stock,category
> 1,Laptop Pro,1299.99,5,Electronics
> 2,Wireless Mouse,29.99,150,Electronics
> 3,Python Book,39.99,75,Education
> 4,Standing Desk,299.99,8,Furniture
> 5,USB Hub,24.99,200,Electronics'''
>
> def parse_csv_to_dicts(csv_text: str) -> list[dict]:
>     reader = csv.reader(StringIO(csv_text))
>     headers = next(reader)   # First row = headers
>     print(f'Headers: {headers}')
>
>     return [
>         dict(zip(headers, row))
>         for row in reader
>         if row  # Skip empty rows
>     ]
>
> records = parse_csv_to_dicts(csv_content)
> print(f'Parsed {len(records)} records')
>
> # Apply type conversion after parsing
> def typed_record(r: dict) -> dict:
>     return {
>         **r,
>         'id':    int(r['id']),
>         'price': float(r['price']),
>         'stock': int(r['stock']),
>     }
>
> typed_records = [typed_record(r) for r in records]
>
> # Now usable as proper typed data
> electronics = [r for r in typed_records if r['category'] == 'Electronics']
> total_value = sum(r['price'] * r['stock'] for r in electronics)
> print(f'Electronics inventory value: ${total_value:,.2f}')
>
> # Using pandas in production:
> # import pandas as pd
> # df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv_content))
> # records = df.to_dict('records')  # Same result!
> ```"

**Scenario 2: "A machine learning pipeline returns feature names and importance scores as separate arrays. Build a sorted feature importance dict."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "ML feature importance — I do this in every model evaluation:
>
> ```python
> import random
>
> # Simulated model output (e.g., from sklearn feature_importances_)
> feature_names = [
>     'age', 'income', 'credit_score', 'debt_ratio',
>     'employment_years', 'num_accounts', 'payment_history',
>     'loan_amount', 'property_value', 'location_score'
> ]
>
> # Simulated importance scores (normally from model.feature_importances_)
> importances = [0.08, 0.22, 0.31, 0.07, 0.11, 0.04, 0.27, 0.05, 0.09, 0.03]
> # Normalize: should sum to ~1.0
> assert abs(sum(importances) - 1.0) < 0.01, 'Importances should sum to 1'
>
> # Build feature importance dict using zip
> feature_importance = {
>     feature: round(importance, 4)
>     for feature, importance in zip(feature_names, importances)
> }
>
> # Sort by importance (descending)
> sorted_importance = dict(
>     sorted(feature_importance.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)
> )
>
> # Report
> print('Feature Importance Report:')
> print('-' * 40)
> cumulative = 0
> for rank, (feature, score) in enumerate(sorted_importance.items(), 1):
>     cumulative += score
>     bar = '█' * int(score * 50)
>     print(f'  {rank:2}. {feature:20} {score:.4f} {bar}')
>
> # Top 5 most important features
> top_5 = dict(list(sorted_importance.items())[:5])
> print(f'\nTop 5 features cover {sum(top_5.values()):.1%} of importance')
>
> # Filter: only features with > 10% importance (significant features)
> significant = {
>     f: imp for f, imp in feature_importance.items()
>     if imp > 0.10
> }
> print(f'Significant features (>10%): {list(significant.keys())}')
> ```"

**Scenario 3: "You're building a web form where field names need to map to their validation rules. Use zip to build the validator config."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Form validation config builder:
>
> ```python
> from typing import Callable
> import re
>
> # Parallel lists defining the form
> field_names = ['username',  'email',         'password',      'age',       'phone']
> field_types = ['str',       'str',           'str',           'int',       'str']
> is_required = [True,        True,            True,            False,       False]
> min_lengths = [3,           5,               8,               None,        10]
> max_lengths = [50,          100,             100,             None,        15]
> patterns    = [
>     r'^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$',        # username: alphanumeric + underscore
>     r'^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[^@]+$',   # email: basic email format
>     r'^(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d).+$',# password: uppercase + digit
>     None,                       # age: no pattern
>     r'^\+?[\d\s\-\(\)]+$',     # phone: digits + formatting chars
> ]
>
> # Build validator config dict using zip
> validator_config = {
>     field: {
>         'type':     ftype,
>         'required': req,
>         'min_len':  min_l,
>         'max_len':  max_l,
>         'pattern':  pat
>     }
>     for field, ftype, req, min_l, max_l, pat
>     in zip(field_names, field_types, is_required, min_lengths, max_lengths, patterns)
> }
>
> def validate_form(data: dict) -> dict:
>     errors = {}
>     for field, rules in validator_config.items():
>         value = data.get(field, '')
>
>         if rules['required'] and not value:
>             errors[field] = f'{field} is required'
>             continue
>
>         if value:
>             if rules['min_len'] and len(str(value)) < rules['min_len']:
>                 errors[field] = f'{field} must be at least {rules[\"min_len\"]} chars'
>             if rules['pattern'] and not re.match(rules['pattern'], str(value)):
>                 errors[field] = f'{field} format is invalid'
>
>     return errors
>
> # Test
> test_data = {'username': 'al', 'email': 'bademail', 'password': 'weakpassword', 'age': 25}
> errors = validate_form(test_data)
> print('Validation errors:', errors)
> # username: must be at least 3 chars
> # email: format is invalid
> # password: format is invalid (no uppercase/digit)
> ```"

sections.title: Dict Comprehension — Nested — Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Conceptual Question:

**Q: When do you use a nested dict comprehension vs breaking it into multiple steps?**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Level):**
> "My rule: if reading the nested comprehension takes more than 5 seconds to understand — break it up. Comprehensions are for clarity, not cleverness.
>
> I use nested comprehensions when: the nesting is shallow (two levels max), the inner and outer logic are independently simple, and the intent is immediately clear.
>
> I break it into steps when: the inner logic has business rules, there are side effects needed, I need to reuse the inner result, or the outer comprehension is already complex.
>
> ```python
> # ACCEPTABLE — clear two-level nesting:
> stats = {
>     dept: {'avg': sum(s)/len(s), 'max': max(s)}
>     for dept, s in dept_scores.items()
> }
>
> # TOO COMPLEX — break into function:
> # Bad:
> result = {
>     dept: {emp: {'salary': s, 'grade': 'A' if s>100000 else 'B' if s>80000 else 'C',
>                  'bonus': s*0.1 if s>100000 else s*0.05}
>            for emp, s in emps.items() if emps}
>     for dept, emps in data.items() if dept != 'Intern'
> }
>
> # Better:
> def compute_employee_stats(salary):
>     return {
>         'salary': salary,
>         'grade':  'A' if salary > 100000 else 'B' if salary > 80000 else 'C',
>         'bonus':  salary * (0.1 if salary > 100000 else 0.05)
>     }
>
> result = {
>     dept: {emp: compute_employee_stats(s) for emp, s in emps.items()}
>     for dept, emps in data.items()
>     if dept != 'Intern'
> }
> ```
>
> The extract-to-function pattern is almost always the right answer for complex inner logic."

### Scenario Questions:

**Scenario 1: "Transform a flat list of database rows into a nested structure grouped by two levels (country → city → users)."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Two-level grouping — classic data reshaping:
>
> ```python
> users = [
>     {'id': 1, 'name': 'Alice', 'country': 'USA', 'city': 'New York'},
>     {'id': 2, 'name': 'Bob',   'country': 'USA', 'city': 'New York'},
>     {'id': 3, 'name': 'Carol', 'country': 'USA', 'city': 'LA'},
>     {'id': 4, 'name': 'Dave',  'country': 'UK',  'city': 'London'},
>     {'id': 5, 'name': 'Eve',   'country': 'UK',  'city': 'London'},
>     {'id': 6, 'name': 'Frank', 'country': 'UK',  'city': 'Manchester'},
> ]
>
> # Get unique countries
> countries = list(set(u['country'] for u in users))
>
> # Two-level nested dict: country → city → list of user names
> geo_tree = {
>     country: {
>         city: [u['name'] for u in users
>                if u['country'] == country and u['city'] == city]
>         for city in set(u['city'] for u in users if u['country'] == country)
>     }
>     for country in countries
> }
>
> import json
> print(json.dumps(geo_tree, indent=2))
> # {
> #   'USA': {
> #     'New York': ['Alice', 'Bob'],
> #     'LA': ['Carol']
> #   },
> #   'UK': {
> #     'London': ['Dave', 'Eve'],
> #     'Manchester': ['Frank']
> #   }
> # }
>
> # More efficient using collections.defaultdict for large datasets:
> from collections import defaultdict
> geo_tree_efficient = defaultdict(lambda: defaultdict(list))
> for u in users:
>     geo_tree_efficient[u['country']][u['city']].append(u['name'])
> # Same result, O(n) instead of O(n²)
> ```"

**Scenario 2: "Build a permission matrix for roles and resources in an RBAC system."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "RBAC permission matrix — I've built this in authorization services:
>
> ```python
> # Define roles and resources
> roles     = ['admin', 'editor', 'viewer', 'guest']
> resources = ['users', 'posts', 'comments', 'settings', 'reports']
>
> # Permission rules (role → set of allowed resources)
> permission_rules = {
>     'admin':  {'users', 'posts', 'comments', 'settings', 'reports'},
>     'editor': {'posts', 'comments', 'reports'},
>     'viewer': {'posts', 'comments', 'reports'},
>     'guest':  {'posts'},
> }
>
> # Build permission matrix: {role: {resource: bool}}
> permission_matrix = {
>     role: {
>         resource: resource in permission_rules.get(role, set())
>         for resource in resources
>     }
>     for role in roles
> }
>
> # Display matrix
> print(f\"{'Role':<10} | \" + ' | '.join(f'{r:8}' for r in resources))
> print('-' * 65)
> for role, perms in permission_matrix.items():
>     row = ' | '.join('✅  YES ' if perms[r] else '❌   NO ' for r in resources)
>     print(f'{role:<10} | {row}')
>
> # Check permission: O(1) lookup
> def can_access(role: str, resource: str) -> bool:
>     return permission_matrix.get(role, {}).get(resource, False)
>
> print(can_access('editor', 'settings'))  # False
> print(can_access('admin', 'settings'))   # True
> print(can_access('viewer', 'reports'))   # True
> ```"

**Scenario 3: "Parse a multi-level JSON API response and create a normalized nested dict for your application."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "JSON normalization — done daily in backend development:
>
> ```python
> # Simulated complex API response
> api_response = {
>     'status': 'success',
>     'data': {
>         'organization': {
>             'id': 'ORG001',
>             'name': 'Acme Corp',
>             'departments': [
>                 {
>                     'dept_id': 'D001',
>                     'dept_name': 'Engineering',
>                     'head_count': 25,
>                     'budget_usd': 2500000,
>                     'teams': [
>                         {'team_id': 'T001', 'team_name': 'Backend',  'size': 8},
>                         {'team_id': 'T002', 'team_name': 'Frontend', 'size': 7},
>                         {'team_id': 'T003', 'team_name': 'DevOps',   'size': 10},
>                     ]
>                 },
>                 {
>                     'dept_id': 'D002',
>                     'dept_name': 'Marketing',
>                     'head_count': 12,
>                     'budget_usd': 800000,
>                     'teams': [
>                         {'team_id': 'T004', 'team_name': 'Digital',  'size': 6},
>                         {'team_id': 'T005', 'team_name': 'Content',  'size': 6},
>                     ]
>                 }
>             ]
>         }
>     }
> }
>
> org_data = api_response['data']['organization']
>
> # Normalize: {dept_name: {team_name: size}}
> dept_team_structure = {
>     dept['dept_name']: {
>         team['team_name']: {
>             'id':     team['team_id'],
>             'size':   team['size'],
>             'budget': round(dept['budget_usd'] * team['size'] / dept['head_count'], 0)
>         }
>         for team in dept['teams']
>     }
>     for dept in org_data['departments']
> }
>
> # Access is now clean
> print(dept_team_structure['Engineering']['Backend'])
> # {'id': 'T001', 'size': 8, 'budget': 800000.0}
>
> # Fast lookups: team_id → full info
> all_teams = {
>     team['team_id']: {
>         **team,
>         'department': dept['dept_name'],
>         'dept_budget': dept['budget_usd']
>     }
>     for dept in org_data['departments']
>     for team in dept['teams']
> }
>
> print(all_teams['T003'])
> # {'team_id': 'T003', 'team_name': 'DevOps', 'size': 10,
> #  'department': 'Engineering', 'dept_budget': 2500000}
> ```"

sections.title: Set Comprehension — Basics — Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Conceptual Question:

**Q: What is a set comprehension, how does it differ from a list comprehension, and when would you choose one over the other?**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Level):**
> "A set comprehension uses `{expression for item in iterable}` — same syntax as list comprehension but with curly braces and no colon. The result is a `set` instead of a `list`, meaning:
>
> - **Duplicates are automatically removed**
> - **Order is not guaranteed** (Python 3.7+ dicts are ordered, but sets are NOT)
> - **Membership testing is O(1)** versus O(n) for lists
> - **Elements must be hashable** (strings, numbers, tuples — not lists or dicts)
>
> I choose set comprehension over list comprehension when:
>
> **1. I need unique values** — fastest deduplication:
> ```python
> # List: [1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3]  → SET: {1, 2, 3}
> unique = {x for x in data}
> # vs list(set(data)) — both work, comprehension allows transformation
> unique_upper = {w.upper() for w in words}  # Transform AND deduplicate
> ```
>
> **2. I need fast membership testing** — building a 'valid values' set:
> ```python
> valid_ids = {record['id'] for record in db_records}
> # Now: user_id in valid_ids  → O(1), not O(n)!
> ```
>
> **3. I need set operations** — intersection, union, difference:
> ```python
> tags_a = {tag for tag in post_a['tags']}
> tags_b = {tag for tag in post_b['tags']}
> common_tags = tags_a & tags_b  # Can't do this with lists!
> ```
>
> I choose list comprehension when order matters, when I might have intentional duplicates, or when I need index access."

### Scenario Questions:

**Scenario 1: "You process 1 million event logs. Each event has a user_id. Find all users who triggered at least one error event."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Set comprehension is perfect here — deduplication is automatic and lookup is O(1):
>
> ```python
> import random
> import time
>
> # Simulate 1M log events
> log_events = [
>     {
>         'event_id': i,
>         'user_id':  f'U{random.randint(1, 10000):05d}',
>         'level':    random.choice(['INFO', 'INFO', 'INFO', 'WARNING', 'ERROR']),
>         'message':  f'Event message {i}'
>     }
>     for i in range(1_000_000)
> ]
>
> # ✅ Set comprehension: unique error users — O(n) scan, O(1) insertion
> start = time.perf_counter()
> error_user_ids = {
>     event['user_id']
>     for event in log_events
>     if event['level'] == 'ERROR'
> }
> elapsed = time.perf_counter() - start
>
> print(f'Scanned 1M events in {elapsed:.2f}s')
> print(f'Unique users with errors: {len(error_user_ids)}')
>
> # Now O(1) membership test for any user:
> def has_error(user_id: str) -> bool:
>     return user_id in error_user_ids  # O(1)!
>
> print(has_error('U00001'))  # True or False instantly
>
> # Compare with bad approach (list — O(n) per lookup):
> # error_user_list = [e['user_id'] for e in log_events if e['level'] == 'ERROR']
> # 'U00001' in error_user_list  ← O(n) every time! Terrible for 1M records
>
> # Production note: for truly large-scale, use Redis SET or
> # a database query: SELECT DISTINCT user_id WHERE level = 'ERROR'
> ```"

**Scenario 2: "You have two lists of product SKUs — one from your warehouse, one from your supplier. Find products that need restocking."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Set operations for inventory management:
>
> ```python
> # Warehouse current inventory (may have duplicates from multiple scans)
> warehouse_scan = [
>     'SKU001', 'SKU002', 'SKU001', 'SKU005', 'SKU008',
>     'SKU002', 'SKU010', 'SKU015', 'SKU005', 'SKU020'
> ]
>
> # Supplier catalog (what we can order)
> supplier_catalog = [
>     'SKU001', 'SKU003', 'SKU005', 'SKU007', 'SKU009',
>     'SKU011', 'SKU013', 'SKU015', 'SKU017', 'SKU019',
>     'SKU021', 'SKU023'
> ]
>
> # Catalog of ALL products we should carry
> required_skus = {f'SKU{i:03d}' for i in range(1, 16)}  # SKU001 to SKU015
>
> # Set comprehensions for analysis
> in_warehouse = {sku for sku in warehouse_scan}
> available_from_supplier = {sku for sku in supplier_catalog}
>
> print(f"In warehouse: {len(in_warehouse)} unique SKUs")
> print(f"From supplier: {len(available_from_supplier)} SKUs")
>
> # Products we're MISSING from warehouse
> missing_from_warehouse = required_skus - in_warehouse
> print(f"\nMissing from warehouse: {sorted(missing_from_warehouse)}")
> # ['SKU003', 'SKU004', 'SKU006', 'SKU007', ...]
>
> # Products we can ORDER from supplier (missing AND available)
> can_restock = missing_from_warehouse & available_from_supplier
> print(f"Can restock from supplier: {sorted(can_restock)}")
>
> # Products missing AND supplier doesn't have (source elsewhere)
> need_new_supplier = missing_from_warehouse - available_from_supplier
> print(f"Need alternative supplier: {sorted(need_new_supplier)}")
>
> # Products in warehouse but not in our required catalog (excess?)
> excess_inventory = in_warehouse - required_skus
> print(f"Excess/unexpected stock: {sorted(excess_inventory)}")
> ```"

**Scenario 3: "Build a 'mutual friends' feature for a social network using set operations."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Social graph set operations — classic interview AND production pattern:
>
> ```python
> from typing import Dict, Set, List
>
> # User friend graphs
> friendships: Dict[str, Set[str]] = {
>     'alice': {'bob', 'carol', 'dave', 'eve', 'frank'},
>     'bob':   {'alice', 'carol', 'grace', 'henry'},
>     'carol': {'alice', 'bob', 'dave', 'grace', 'ivan'},
>     'dave':  {'alice', 'carol', 'eve', 'judy'},
>     'eve':   {'alice', 'dave', 'frank', 'judy'},
>     'frank': {'alice', 'eve', 'grace'},
>     'grace': {'bob', 'carol', 'frank'},
>     'henry': {'bob', 'ivan'},
>     'ivan':  {'carol', 'henry'},
>     'judy':  {'dave', 'eve'},
> }
>
> def mutual_friends(user1: str, user2: str) -> Set[str]:
>     '''O(min(n,m)) — set intersection'''
>     return friendships.get(user1, set()) & friendships.get(user2, set())
>
> def suggested_friends(user: str, limit: int = 5) -> List[dict]:
>     '''
>     Friends-of-friends not already friends with user.
>     Ranked by number of mutual friends.
>     '''
>     user_friends = friendships.get(user, set())
>
>     # All friends-of-friends (2 hops away)
>     friends_of_friends = {
>         fof
>         for friend in user_friends
>         for fof in friendships.get(friend, set())
>         if fof != user and fof not in user_friends  # Not self, not already friend
>     }
>
>     # Rank by mutual friends count
>     suggestions = [
>         {
>             'user': candidate,
>             'mutual_friends': mutual_friends(user, candidate),
>             'mutual_count': len(mutual_friends(user, candidate))
>         }
>         for candidate in friends_of_friends
>     ]
>
>     return sorted(suggestions, key=lambda x: x['mutual_count'], reverse=True)[:limit]
>
> # Test
> print(f"Alice & Bob mutual friends: {mutual_friends('alice', 'bob')}")
> # {'carol'}
>
> print(f"\nFriend suggestions for Henry:")
> for s in suggested_friends('henry'):
>     print(f"  {s['user']:8} — {s['mutual_count']} mutual: {s['mutual_friends']}")
> # ivan     — 1 mutual: {'bob'}
> # carol    — 1 mutual: {'ivan'} ... etc
> ```"

sections.title: Set Comprehension — Deduplication Patterns — Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Conceptual Question:

**Q: When deduplicating records, what is the difference between using a set comprehension vs using `list(set(data))`, and when does each approach fail?**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Level):**
> "Both remove duplicates, but they have different capabilities and failure modes:
>
> **`list(set(data))`** — works for simple hashable values (strings, numbers, tuples). Fails for:
> - **Dicts** (unhashable): `list(set([{'a': 1}, {'a': 1}]))` → `TypeError`
> - **Lists** (unhashable): same problem
> - When you need to **normalize before deduplicating**: `list(set(['Hello', 'hello']))` keeps both!
>
> **Set comprehension** — more powerful because you can **transform in the expression**:
> ```python
> # Normalize AND deduplicate in one operation:
> unique = {email.lower().strip() for email in emails}
>
> # Extract a field AND deduplicate:
> unique_depts = {emp['department'] for emp in employees}
> # This works even though employees are dicts (unhashable)!
>
> # Dedup by a derived key:
> unique_domains = {email.split('@')[1] for email in emails}
> ```
>
> **When set comprehension fails**:
> - The expression produces an **unhashable type** (list or dict in the expression position):
>   ```python
>   # WRONG — lists are unhashable:
>   {list(range(3)) for x in data}  # TypeError!
>
>   # RIGHT — use tuples:
>   {tuple(range(3)) for x in data}  # Works!
>   ```
>
> **My production rule**: use `{normalize(x) for x in data}` for deduplication — it handles transformation and dedup in one pass. Only use `list(set(data))` for simple lists of primitives where no normalization is needed."

### Scenario Questions:

**Scenario 1: "You merge customer data from 3 databases. Each may have different formatting (case, spaces). Deduplicate properly."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Multi-source customer deduplication with normalization:
>
> ```python
> from typing import List, Dict
> import re
>
> def normalize_email(email: str) -> str:
>     '''Normalize email for deduplication'''
>     if not email:
>         return ''
>     return email.strip().lower()
>
> def normalize_phone(phone: str) -> str:
>     '''Remove all non-digits for comparison'''
>     return re.sub(r'\D', '', str(phone))
>
> # Three database exports
> db_sources = [
>     [  # CRM Database
>         {'email': 'Alice@Company.COM', 'phone': '(555) 123-4567', 'source': 'crm'},
>         {'email': 'bob@company.com',   'phone': '555-987-6543',   'source': 'crm'},
>     ],
>     [  # Marketing Database
>         {'email': 'alice@company.com', 'phone': '5551234567',     'source': 'marketing'},
>         {'email': 'CAROL@COMPANY.COM', 'phone': '555.246.8100',   'source': 'marketing'},
>     ],
>     [  # Support Database
>         {'email': ' bob@company.com ', 'phone': '+1-555-987-6543','source': 'support'},
>         {'email': 'dave@company.com',  'phone': '555-369-1212',   'source': 'support'},
>     ]
> ]
>
> all_customers = [c for source in db_sources for c in source]
> print(f"Total records: {len(all_customers)}")
>
> # Unique normalized emails (for ID)
> unique_emails = {normalize_email(c['email']) for c in all_customers if c['email']}
> print(f"Unique customers by email: {len(unique_emails)}")
>
> # Full deduplication: keep first occurrence per email
> seen_emails = set()
> deduplicated = []
> for customer in all_customers:
>     norm_email = normalize_email(customer['email'])
>     if norm_email and norm_email not in seen_emails:
>         seen_emails.add(norm_email)
>         deduplicated.append({
>             **customer,
>             'email': norm_email,  # Store normalized version
>             'phone': normalize_phone(customer['phone'])
>         })
>
> print(f"After dedup: {len(deduplicated)} unique customers")
> for c in deduplicated:
>     print(f"  {c['email']}: {c['phone']} (first seen in: {c['source']})")
> ```"

**Scenario 2: "Remove duplicate API responses that might be returned by a retry mechanism."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Idempotent deduplication for retry systems:
>
> ```python
> import hashlib
> import json
> from typing import List, Dict
>
> def response_fingerprint(response: dict) -> str:
>     '''
>     Create a unique fingerprint for an API response.
>     Excludes timestamp fields that change on retry.
>     '''
>     # Fields that identify uniqueness (not timestamps!)
>     stable_fields = {
>         k: v for k, v in response.items()
>         if k not in ('timestamp', 'request_id', 'retry_count', 'received_at')
>     }
>     return hashlib.md5(
>         json.dumps(stable_fields, sort_keys=True).encode()
>     ).hexdigest()
>
> # Simulated API responses with retries (duplicates!)
> api_responses = [
>     {'order_id': 'O001', 'status': 'completed', 'amount': 99.99, 'timestamp': '10:01:00', 'retry_count': 0},
>     {'order_id': 'O002', 'status': 'pending',   'amount': 49.99, 'timestamp': '10:01:05', 'retry_count': 0},
>     {'order_id': 'O001', 'status': 'completed', 'amount': 99.99, 'timestamp': '10:01:10', 'retry_count': 1},  # Retry!
>     {'order_id': 'O003', 'status': 'failed',    'amount': 24.99, 'timestamp': '10:01:15', 'retry_count': 0},
>     {'order_id': 'O002', 'status': 'pending',   'amount': 49.99, 'timestamp': '10:01:20', 'retry_count': 1},  # Retry!
>     {'order_id': 'O001', 'status': 'completed', 'amount': 99.99, 'timestamp': '10:01:25', 'retry_count': 2},  # Retry!
> ]
>
> # Deduplicate using fingerprint set
> seen_fingerprints = set()
> unique_responses = []
> for response in api_responses:
>     fp = response_fingerprint(response)
>     if fp not in seen_fingerprints:
>         seen_fingerprints.add(fp)
>         unique_responses.append(response)
>
> print(f"Raw responses: {len(api_responses)}")
> print(f"Unique responses: {len(unique_responses)}")
> for r in unique_responses:
>     print(f"  Order {r['order_id']}: {r['status']} (${r['amount']})")
>
> # In production: store fingerprints in Redis with TTL
> # redis.set(f'processed:{fp}', '1', ex=3600)  # 1-hour dedup window
> ```"

**Scenario 3: "Find users who are in ALL three permission groups (must appear in all three lists)."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Multi-group intersection — classic access control pattern:
>
> ```python
> # Permission groups (users must be in ALL groups for full access)
> beta_testers   = {'alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dave', 'eve', 'frank'}
> premium_users  = {'alice', 'carol', 'eve', 'grace', 'henry', 'ivan'}
> verified_users = {'alice', 'bob', 'eve', 'grace', 'judy', 'kevin'}
>
> # Users who are beta testers
> beta_set    = {uid for uid in beta_testers}
> premium_set = {uid for uid in premium_users}
> verified_set= {uid for uid in verified_users}
>
> # In ALL three groups → intersection
> all_three = beta_set & premium_set & verified_set
> print(f"Users in ALL 3 groups: {all_three}")
> # {'alice', 'eve'}
>
> # In at least TWO groups
> in_beta_and_premium   = beta_set & premium_set
> in_beta_and_verified  = beta_set & verified_set
> in_premium_and_verified = premium_set & verified_set
> in_at_least_two = in_beta_and_premium | in_beta_and_verified | in_premium_and_verified
> print(f"In at least 2 groups: {in_at_least_two}")
>
> # Progressive permission levels
> def get_access_level(user_id: str) -> str:
>     in_beta     = user_id in beta_set
>     in_premium  = user_id in premium_set
>     in_verified = user_id in verified_set
>     count = sum([in_beta, in_premium, in_verified])
>
>     return (
>         'FULL_ACCESS'    if count == 3 else
>         'ELEVATED'       if count == 2 else
>         'BASIC'          if count == 1 else
>         'NO_ACCESS'
>     )
>
> test_users = ['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'grace', 'judy', 'unknown']
> for user in test_users:
>     print(f"  {user:10}: {get_access_level(user)}")
> ```"

sections.title: Set Comprehension — with Conditions — Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Conceptual Question:

**Q: What are the advantages of using a set for membership testing compared to a list, and how does a set comprehension with conditions help build these efficiently?**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Level):**
> "Set membership testing `x in my_set` is O(1) — constant time regardless of set size. List membership `x in my_list` is O(n) — linear scan. For large collections this difference is enormous:
>
> ```python
> import time
> big_list = list(range(1_000_000))
> big_set  = set(range(1_000_000))
>
> # O(n): ~50ms for worst case
> 999999 in big_list   # Has to scan all 1M items
>
> # O(1): ~0.001ms regardless of set size
> 999999 in big_set    # Direct hash lookup!
> ```
>
> Set comprehension with conditions lets you build filtered, deduplicated lookup structures in one pass:
>
> ```python
> # One pass through data → filtered + deduplicated + O(1) lookup
> active_user_ids = {u['id'] for u in users if u['active'] and u['verified']}
>
> # Now every permission check is O(1):
> if request.user_id in active_user_ids:
>     grant_access()
>
> # Compare: without this, every check is O(n):
> active_users_list = [u for u in users if u['active'] and u['verified']]
> # request.user_id in [u['id'] for u in active_users_list]  ← O(n) every time!
> ```
>
> In production APIs, I always build set-based lookup structures at startup or cache warm-up time for any 'is this valid?' checks — valid tokens, active user IDs, allowed IP addresses, valid product SKUs. The O(1) lookup vs O(n) scan difference is critical at scale."

### Scenario Questions:

**Scenario 1: "Build an IP allowlist and blocklist system using set comprehensions for a security middleware."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "IP filtering with sets — classic security pattern:
>
> ```python
> import ipaddress
> from typing import Set
>
> # Simulated database/config data
> raw_allowlist = [
>     '192.168.1.100', '10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.2', '192.168.1.100',  # Dup!
>     '172.16.0.50', '10.0.0.3', '8.8.8.8', '8.8.4.4',
> ]
> raw_blocklist = [
>     '192.168.1.200', '10.0.0.99', '1.2.3.4', '5.6.7.8',
>     '192.168.1.200',  # Dup!
>     '10.0.0.99',      # Dup!
> ]
>
> def is_valid_ip(ip: str) -> bool:
>     try:
>         ipaddress.ip_address(ip.strip())
>         return True
>     except ValueError:
>         return False
>
> # Build filtered, deduplicated sets in one expression
> ALLOWLIST: Set[str] = {
>     ip.strip()
>     for ip in raw_allowlist
>     if is_valid_ip(ip.strip())
> }
> BLOCKLIST: Set[str] = {
>     ip.strip()
>     for ip in raw_blocklist
>     if is_valid_ip(ip.strip())
> }
>
> # Sanity check: IPs shouldn't be in both
> conflicts = ALLOWLIST & BLOCKLIST
> if conflicts:
>     raise ValueError(f'IPs in both allow and block list: {conflicts}')
>
> print(f'Allowlist: {len(ALLOWLIST)} IPs (deduplicated from {len(raw_allowlist)})')
> print(f'Blocklist: {len(BLOCKLIST)} IPs (deduplicated from {len(raw_blocklist)})')
>
> # Middleware check — O(1) per lookup
> def check_request(client_ip: str) -> dict:
>     ip = client_ip.strip()
>     if ip in BLOCKLIST:
>         return {'allowed': False, 'reason': 'IP is blocked'}
>     if ALLOWLIST and ip not in ALLOWLIST:
>         return {'allowed': False, 'reason': 'IP not in allowlist'}
>     return {'allowed': True, 'reason': 'IP cleared'}
>
> # Test
> test_ips = ['10.0.0.1', '10.0.0.99', '99.99.99.99', '8.8.8.8']
> for ip in test_ips:
>     result = check_request(ip)
>     status = '✅' if result['allowed'] else '🚫'
>     print(f'  {status} {ip:15}: {result[\"reason\"]}')
> ```"

**Scenario 2: "Find all unique error types from a month of production logs, filtered by severity level, for an incident report."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Production log analysis with set comprehensions:
>
> ```python
> import random
> from datetime import datetime, timedelta
>
> # Simulate a month of production logs
> ERROR_TYPES = [
>     'DatabaseTimeout', 'DatabaseTimeout', 'DatabaseTimeout',  # Common
>     'APIRateLimit', 'APIRateLimit',
>     'PaymentFailed', 'NetworkTimeout', 'AuthenticationError',
>     'InvalidInput', 'ResourceNotFound', 'InternalServerError',
>     'CacheEviction', 'QueueFull', 'CircuitBreakerOpen',
> ]
> SERVICES = ['api', 'worker', 'scheduler', 'payment', 'auth']
> LEVELS   = ['DEBUG', 'INFO', 'INFO', 'WARNING', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL']
>
> # Generate 10,000 log entries
> logs = [
>     {
>         'timestamp': datetime.now() - timedelta(days=random.randint(0, 30)),
>         'level':     random.choice(LEVELS),
>         'error_type': random.choice(ERROR_TYPES),
>         'service':   random.choice(SERVICES),
>         'count':     random.randint(1, 100),
>     }
>     for _ in range(10000)
> ]
>
> # Unique critical error types (for immediate action)
> critical_errors = {
>     log['error_type']
>     for log in logs
>     if log['level'] == 'CRITICAL'
> }
> print(f"Critical error types ({len(critical_errors)}):")
> for e in sorted(critical_errors):
>     print(f"  🔴 {e}")
>
> # Unique services with ERROR or CRITICAL events
> problematic_services = {
>     log['service']
>     for log in logs
>     if log['level'] in ('ERROR', 'CRITICAL')
> }
> print(f"\nAffected services: {problematic_services}")
>
> # Unique (service, error_type) pairs for root cause matrix
> error_matrix = {
>     (log['service'], log['error_type'])
>     for log in logs
>     if log['level'] in ('ERROR', 'CRITICAL')
> }
> print(f"\nUnique service+error combinations: {len(error_matrix)}")
>
> # Services that had PaymentFailed errors
> payment_issue_services = {
>     service for service, error in error_matrix
>     if error == 'PaymentFailed'
> }
> print(f"Services with PaymentFailed: {payment_issue_services}")
> ```"

**Scenario 3: "You process customer order files daily. Find customers who ordered on EVERY day this week (loyalty detection)."**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Multi-day intersection for loyalty detection:
>
> ```python
> from datetime import date
>
> # Daily order data (simulated — each day's orders)
> daily_orders = {
>     date(2024, 1, 15): ['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'dave', 'alice'],
>     date(2024, 1, 16): ['alice', 'carol', 'eve', 'frank', 'carol'],
>     date(2024, 1, 17): ['alice', 'bob', 'carol', 'grace', 'alice'],
>     date(2024, 1, 18): ['alice', 'carol', 'henry', 'eve'],
>     date(2024, 1, 19): ['alice', 'carol', 'ivan', 'dave'],
> }
>
> # Daily unique customers (set comprehension per day)
> daily_unique_customers = {
>     day: {customer for customer in customers}
>     for day, customers in daily_orders.items()
> }
>
> print("Daily unique customers:")
> for day, customers in daily_unique_customers.items():
>     print(f"  {day}: {sorted(customers)}")
>
> # Customers who ordered on EVERY day (intersection of all days)
> all_days = list(daily_unique_customers.values())
> loyal_customers = all_days[0].intersection(*all_days[1:])
> print(f"\nOrdered EVERY day this week: {loyal_customers}")
> # {'alice', 'carol'}
>
> # Customers who ordered on AT LEAST 3 days
> from collections import Counter
> all_customer_days = Counter(
>     customer
>     for customers in daily_unique_customers.values()
>     for customer in customers
> )
> frequent_shoppers = {
>     customer for customer, days in all_customer_days.items()
>     if days >= 3
> }
> print(f"Ordered 3+ days: {frequent_shoppers}")
>
> # New customers (only appeared ONCE all week)
> one_time = {c for c, count in all_customer_days.items() if count == 1}
> print(f"One-time customers: {one_time}")
> ```"

sections.title: Generator Expressions — What & Why — Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Conceptual Question:

**Q: What is a generator expression? How does it differ from a list comprehension, and when do you choose one over the other?**

**✅ Answer (5-Year Experience Level):**
> "A generator expression uses `(expr for item in iterable)` — parentheses instead of brackets. It returns a **generator object**, which is a lazy iterator: values are computed **one at a time, on demand**, rather than all upfront.
>
> Key differences:
>
> | | List Comprehension | Generator Expression |
> |---|---|---|
> | Memory | O(n) — all items | O(1) — one at a time |
> | Speed | Faster for repeated access | Faster when not all items needed |
> | Reusable | Yes — iterate many times | No — exhausted after one pass |
> | Indexable | Yes — `result[i]` | No — TypeError |
> | Has `len()` | Yes | No |
>
> **I choose generator when:**
> - Processing large datasets where RAM matters (logs, CSV files, database cursors)
> - Passing to a single-pass function: `sum()`, `any()`, `all()`, `max()`, `join()`
> - Building lazy pipelines where not all values may be needed
> - Streaming data processing (process as data arrives)
>
> **I choose list comprehension when:**
> - I need to iterate the result multiple times
> - I need random access (`result[i]`)
> - I need `len(result)` before processing
> - The dataset is small enough that memory isn't a concern
>
> Real example from production: processing a 50GB log file:
> ```python
> # List comprehension: tries to load 50GB into RAM → crash!
> errors = [line for line in open('huge.log') if 'ERROR' in line]
>
> # Generator: processes line by line, uses ~1KB RAM
> errors = (line for line in open('huge.log') if 'ERROR' in line)
> error_count = sum(1 for _ in errors)  # Counts without loading!
> ```"

### Scenario Questions:

**Scenario 1: "Process a 10GB CSV file to calculate the average transaction amount. How do you avoid loading it all into memory?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Generator pipeline for large file processing:
>
> ```python
> import csv
> from io import StringIO
>
> # Simulate a large CSV (in production: real file path)
> csv_data = 'id,amount,status\n' + '\n'.join(
>     f'{i},{i*10.50},{"completed" if i%3!=0 else "refunded"}'
>     for i in range(1, 100001)
> )
>
> def calculate_stats_streaming(csv_content):
>     '''
>     Calculate stats without loading entire file into memory.
>     Uses generators for O(1) memory.
>     '''
>     reader = csv.DictReader(StringIO(csv_content))
>
>     # Generator: parse amount for completed transactions only
>     amounts = (
>         float(row['amount'])
>         for row in reader
>         if row['status'] == 'completed'
>     )
>
>     # Single-pass statistics (Welford's online algorithm)
>     count = 0
>     total = 0.0
>     min_amt = float('inf')
>     max_amt = float('-inf')
>
>     for amount in amounts:  # Single pass through generator
>         count += 1
>         total += amount
>         min_amt = min(min_amt, amount)
>         max_amt = max(max_amt, amount)
>
>     if count == 0:
>         return None
>
>     return {
>         'count': count,
>         'total': round(total, 2),
>         'average': round(total / count, 2),
>         'min': min_amt,
>         'max': max_amt,
>     }
>
> stats = calculate_stats_streaming(csv_data)
> print(f'Transaction stats: {stats}')
>

> #                    if row['status'] == 'completed')

> # Memory used: O(1) regardless of file size!
> ```"

**Scenario 2: "You're building a real-time log monitoring system. How do you process incoming log lines efficiently?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Streaming log processing with generator pipeline:
>
> ```python
> import time
> import random
> from collections import deque
>
> # Simulated log stream (in production: tail -f / Kafka / CloudWatch)
> def log_stream(num_lines=50):
>     '''Simulate a streaming log source'''
>     levels = ['DEBUG', 'INFO', 'INFO', 'INFO', 'WARNING', 'ERROR', 'CRITICAL']
>     services = ['api', 'worker', 'auth', 'payment']
>     messages = {
>         'DEBUG': 'Processing request',
>         'INFO': 'Request completed successfully',
>         'WARNING': 'Response time above threshold',
>         'ERROR': 'Database connection failed',
>         'CRITICAL': 'Service unavailable',
>     }
>     for i in range(num_lines):
>         level = random.choice(levels)
>         yield {
>             'line_num': i + 1,
>             'timestamp': time.time(),
>             'level': level,
>             'service': random.choice(services),
>             'message': messages[level],
>         }
>
> # Generator pipeline — each stage is lazy
> def parse_logs(stream):
>     return (log for log in stream)
>
> def filter_errors(parsed):
>     return (log for log in parsed if log['level'] in ('ERROR', 'CRITICAL'))
>
> def format_alert(errors):
>     return (
>         f"🚨 [{log['level']}] {log['service']}: {log['message']}"
>         for log in errors
>     )
>
> # Connect the pipeline — nothing executes yet!
> raw_stream   = log_stream(num_lines=100)
> parsed       = parse_logs(raw_stream)
> errors_only  = filter_errors(parsed)
> alerts       = format_alert(errors_only)
>
> # NOW execute — processes one line at a time through all stages
> print("Real-time alerts:")
> alert_count = 0
> for alert in alerts:
>     print(f"  {alert}")
>     alert_count += 1
>
> print(f"\nTotal alerts generated: {alert_count}")
> # Memory used: O(1) — only one log line in memory at a time!
> ```"

**Scenario 3: "Compare performance of generator vs list comprehension for a data pipeline. When does each win?"**

**✅ Answer:**
> "Benchmarking generators vs lists — context determines the winner:
>
> ```python
> import time
> import sys
>
> N = 1_000_000
>
> # BENCHMARK 1: Single-pass sum — GENERATOR WINS (no list built)
> print('=== Benchmark 1: sum() — single pass ===')
> start = time.perf_counter()
> result_list = sum([x**2 for x in range(N)])
> list_time = time.perf_counter() - start
>
> start = time.perf_counter()
> result_gen = sum(x**2 for x in range(N))
> gen_time = time.perf_counter() - start
>
> print(f'List: {list_time:.3f}s | Generator: {gen_time:.3f}s')
> print(f'Generator is {list_time/gen_time:.1f}x faster for sum()')
>
> # BENCHMARK 2: Multiple iterations — LIST WINS
> print('\n=== Benchmark 2: iterate 3 times — list wins ===')
> data_list = [x**2 for x in range(N)]
>
> start = time.perf_counter()
> s1 = sum(data_list)
> s2 = max(data_list)
> s3 = min(data_list)
> list_multi_time = time.perf_counter() - start
>
> start = time.perf_counter()
> s1 = sum(x**2 for x in range(N))    # Rebuilds each time!
> s2 = max(x**2 for x in range(N))
> s3 = min(x**2 for x in range(N))
> gen_multi_time = time.perf_counter() - start
>
> print(f'List (3 passes): {list_multi_time:.3f}s')
> print(f'Generator (3×rebuild): {gen_multi_time:.3f}s')
> print(f'List is {gen_multi_time/list_multi_time:.1f}x faster for multiple passes!')
>
> # BENCHMARK 3: Memory — GENERATOR WINS dramatically
> print('\n=== Benchmark 3: Memory comparison ===')
> list_mem = sys.getsizeof([x**2 for x in range(N)])
> gen_mem  = sys.getsizeof(x**2 for x in range(N))
> print(f'List memory: {list_mem:,} bytes ({list_mem/1024/1024:.1f} MB)')
> print(f'Gen memory:  {gen_mem:,} bytes ({gen_mem} bytes!)')
> print(f'List uses {list_mem//gen_mem:,}× more memory')
>
> print('\n📌 Decision rule:')
> print('  Single pass (sum/any/all/join) → GENERATOR ✅')
> print('  Multiple passes needed         → LIST ✅')
> print('  Large data, memory limited     → GENERATOR ✅')
> print('  Need random access (indexing)  → LIST ✅')
> ```"
